claims.text: Engineering nanoscale precipitates in refractory high-entropy alloys can improve high-temperature mechanical capability.
Nanoscale precipitate engineering can limit density while improving high-temperature capability.
Nanoscale precipitate engineering can preserve room-temperature performance.
Obstruction of dislocation movement by nanoscale precipitates enhances high-temperature strength.
Obstruction of dislocation movement by nanoscale precipitates enhances high-temperature creep resistance.
Nanoscale precipitates can enhance high-temperature strength and creep resistance without significantly compromising room-temperature ductility.
The proposed benefit should hold above 1000°C under applied stress above 500 MPa.
Temperatures above 1000°C and stresses above 500 MPa are typical jet-turbine application conditions.
At 1000°C, nanoscale precipitate engineering will increase yield strength by at least 10% relative to an alloy without such engineering.
At 1000°C, nanoscale precipitate engineering will improve creep resistance by a factor of two relative to an alloy without such engineering.
Nanoscale precipitate engineering will maintain or slightly improve room-temperature performance relative to the baseline alloy.
Current manufacturing techniques limit uniform control of nanoscale-precipitate distribution, size, and composition.

contradictions.description: The stated domain is above 1000°C, but the quantitative prediction and experiment are set at exactly 1000°C.
The stated loading domain is stress above 500 MPa, whereas the proposed creep test uses exactly 500 MPa.

The prediction requires at least a 10% yield-strength gain and a twofold creep-resistance gain, but falsification is triggered only below 5% improvement. Results between these thresholds would fail the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
